Formar o genitivo singular e plural e us: Form the genitive singular and plural and use it for absence, possession, quantity, origin and the most frequent prepositions.
(ou: o caso da origem — e a primeira met: (or: the case of origin — and the first half of the most famous case in Russian)
Uma cena que você já viveu (ou vai viver: Picture a scene you will probably live. You are in Russia, in a shop, and you want to say that you have no money. You think: "money in Russian is де́ньги, so I will say у меня́ нет де́ньги." The person looks at you and corrects: — У меня́ нет де́нег. You stare. It is the same word, де́ньги, but now it is де́нег, with no -и at the end. You wonder: "Haven't I already changed this word once? Why did it change again? How many forms does it have?" This happens to every learner of Russian the first time they meet the genitive, and it is where many give up. Let me be honest: this is the most complex case in Russian. But in this lesson I will do two things. STEP 1: I will explain the genitive so clearly that it looks simple. STEP 2: I will split the genitive over two lessons so you do not quit halfway. This is lesson 27: the genitive as "of" and as negation. Only that: no plural, no numbers, no prepositions; those wait for lesson 28. And before we begin, some reassurance: you are finishing the tedious part of Russian. The essential grammar ends here. What comes next is not harder, it is richer. First, what does "genitive" mean? A little etymology helps. The word comes from Latin genitivus, a Latin version of a Greek term meaning the case of the "kind" or "family" something belongs to; it is related to genus, to gignere ("to beget") and to the words gene and genetics. So the genitive is the case of origin and belonging. When you say "Ivan's book", you are saying that the book belongs to Ivan, comes from Ivan, is tied to Ivan. Unlike many languages, English has two ways to do this: "of" (the book of the teacher, the centre of the city, the colour of the sea) and the ending 's (Ivan's book, my mother's house). Look: in all these phrases the "of" or the 's shows possession, belonging or origin. That is what the genitive does in Russian. It is the case of "of" and of 's. And genetics is a nice memory hook: the genitive is the "genetic case" of the sentence, the case that marks whom a thing comes from.
Genitivo singular: o «de» e as terminaçõ: Genitive singular: the "of" and the endings
A ponte com o português. Antes de qualqu: A bridge with English. Before any table, let us build the bridge. English expresses the genitive in two ways. Way 1, with "of": the book of Ivan. The house of my mother. Way 2, with 's: Ivan's book. My mother's house. In Russian, this is where the two meet: there is no separate word "of" and no 's. What exists is a change in the ending of the noun. Кни́га Ива́на is literally "book Ivan-of" (Ivan with the genitive ending). That is why the case is called the genitive: it marks origin, possession, belonging, with no word "of", only with an ending. The endings of the genitive singular. Now the endings. The method is the same as always: STEP 1: find the nominative form (the dictionary form). STEP 2: add the genitive ending, which depends on the gender and on the ending of the word. STEP 3: done, the noun is in the genitive. Notice: masculine and neuter take -А/-Я. Feminine takes -Ы/-И (or -ИИ after -ия). Neuter in -мя takes -ЕНИ. That is all. Let us see each case in detail.
As terminações do genitivo singular: The endings of the genitive singular
-Ы (ou -И depois de г, к, х, ж, ч, ш, щ): -Ы (or -И after г, к, х, ж, ч, ш, щ)
O MASCULINO no genitivo. Masculino em co: The MASCULINE in the genitive. Masculine in a consonant → -А. Notice: the -А is added at the end of the word. Masculine in -й → -Я. Notice: the -й disappears and -Я comes in. Masculine in -ь → -Я. Notice: the -ь disappears and -Я comes in. Watch the stress: слова́рь → словаря́ (stress on the ending), but учи́тель → учи́теля (stress on the stem). There is no fixed rule. You have to listen and memorise.
O genitivo responde a «кого? чего?» (de: The genitive answers «кого? чего?» (of whom? of what?). It is the most used case in Russian. Singular (seen already): -а → -ы; -я → -и; consonant → -а; masculine -й and -ь → -я; -о → -а; -е → -я; feminine -ь → -и. After г, к, х, ж, ч, ш, щ write -и. Plural: masculine: consonant → -ов (стол → столов); -й → -ев (музей → музеев); -ь, ж, ч, ш, щ → -ей (словарь → словарей, врач → врачей). Feminine and neuter: the ending disappears (zero): книга → книг, окно → окон. But -я → -ь (неделя → недель) and -ие → -ий. Sometimes a fleeting vowel appears: сестра → сестёр, девушка → девушек. Irregular: друзья → друзей, дети → детей, люди → людей, семья → семей.
o português usa «de» para tudo («livro d: English uses «of» for almost everything («the brother's book», «without books»). In Russian the word changes its ending instead of getting an «of».

A primeira aplicação: a NEGAÇÃO (\"não t: The first use: NEGATION ("I don't have")

The first use: NEGATION ("I don't have"). Now that you know the endings, here is the first practical use, and it is good news: the negation of possession is the gateway to the genitive. It is the easiest and most frequent use. You already know from lesson 6 how to say "I have": У меня́ есть кни́га. (I have a book.) To say "I don't have a book", Russian swaps есть for нет and puts the object in the genitive: У меня́ нет кни́ги. (I have no book.) Notice: кни́га became кни́ги. That is the genitive singular. Compare. The logic is simple: Есть (have) + nominative. Нет (don't have) + genitive. Why the genitive? Here is a handy way to picture it: if I have a book, the book is mine, it belongs to me. If I don't have it, nothing belongs to me, and the genitive, the case of belonging, marks that missing belonging. English has a faint hint of this idea in "I have no book", where "no" works like "not any" and you are left with the empty set. Full sentences with "I don't have". Notice: all the objects are in the genitive, every one of them. It is a fixed rule: нет always takes the genitive. Careful: some of these sentences have a genitive plural (друзе́й, дете́й, де́нег). That belongs to lesson 28. For now focus on the genitive singular; the singular sentences are the easiest.
We do not have a house.
Seis usos. (1) Ausência, com «нет»: «У м: Six uses. (1) Absence, with «нет»: «У меня нет времени». (2) Quantity: «много, мало, несколько, сколько, достаточно» + genitive plural for countable things (много книг) and genitive singular for what cannot be counted (много воды). (3) Measures and containers: «килограмм хлеба, литр молока, бутылка воды, чашка чая, кусок сыра». (4) Owner: «книга брата». (5) Prepositions: у, из, от, до, после, для, без, около, вокруг. (6) Origin and exit: «из» and «с» + genitive answer «откуда?» (where from?) and are the opposite of «в» and «на»: в школу → из школы; на работу → с работы.
Com «много» e coisas contáveis use o gen: With «много» and countable things use the genitive plural.

A segunda aplicação: a POSSE (\"o livro: The second use: POSSESSION ("the book of...")

The second use of the genitive is possession. It is the English "of" or 's. Compare. Notice: in Russian the first noun (the thing owned) stays in the nominative. The second noun (the owner) goes into the genitive. The "of" is not a separate word; it is the ending of the second noun. Structure: [thing owned, nominative] + [owner, genitive]. Examples in full sentences. Notice: the first noun (кни́га, дом, и́мя, центр, цвет, му́зыка, кры́ша, дверь) stays in the nominative. The second noun (Ива́на, ма́мы, ма́льчика, го́рода, мо́ря, компози́тора, до́ма, ко́мнаты) goes into the genitive. It is the owner. The magic question is "whose is it?" and the answer goes into the genitive. "Whose book? Ivan's." → Ива́на. Careful with the order: English can say "Ivan's book" (owner first), but Russian always puts the thing first and the owner after it, like English "the book of Ivan".

O uso do genitivo com \"нет\" em frases: The genitive with "нет" in sentences without у меня

The word нет can also be used without у меня. It then means "there is not", "there is no". Notice: the object still goes into the genitive. Нет always takes the genitive, whether or not there is a «у меня». In context:
Os erros que o brasileiro VAI cometer no: The mistakes English speakers WILL make with the genitive. Mistake 1: using the nominative instead of the genitive after «нет». Wrong: У меня́ нет кни́га. Right: У меня́ нет кни́ги. Нет always takes the genitive, without exception. Mistake 2: forgetting that feminine -а becomes -ы (or -и after г, к, х, ж, ч, ш, щ). Wrong: У меня́ нет кни́гы. Right: У меня́ нет кни́ги. (кни́га has a г before the -а, so it is -и.) Mistake 3: forgetting that feminine -я becomes -и. Wrong: У меня́ нет семья́. Right: У меня́ нет семьи́. Mistake 4: forgetting that feminine -ь becomes -и. Wrong: У меня́ нет дверь. Right: У меня́ нет две́ри. Mistake 5: forgetting that -ия becomes -ии. Wrong: Э́то центр Росси́е. Right: Э́то центр Росси́и (-ия always becomes -ии). Mistake 6: forgetting that -мя becomes -мени. Wrong: У меня́ нет вре́мя. Right: У меня́ нет вре́мени. Mistake 7: confusing the genitive with the animate accusative. For masculine animate nouns the genitive and the accusative have the same form (-а/-я), so it is easy to mix them up. But the function differs. Accusative: the object of the action. Я ви́жу дру́га. (I see my friend.) Genitive: possession or negation. У меня́ нет дру́га. (I have no friend.) The form is the same but the context is different. Don't worry about telling them apart for now; just know that after нет it is always genitive. Mistake 8: putting the thing owned in the genitive instead of the owner. Wrong: Ива́н кни́га (meaning "Ivan's book"). Right: Кни́га Ива́на. The thing owned (кни́га) stays in the nominative. The owner (Ива́н) goes into the genitive (Ива́на). Mistake 9: thinking every English "of" becomes a genitive. English "of" has many senses: possession ("the book of Ivan"), origin ("I am from Chicago"), material ("a table of wood"), subject ("we speak of music"). In Russian each sense has its own structure. The genitive covers possession and some origins. But "a wooden table" is an adjective (деревя́нный стол), not a genitive. For now, focus on the genitive of possession. Mistake 10: getting the stress wrong. Some words move their stress in the genitive: окно́ → окна́ (the stress moves), вода́ → воды́ (the stress moves), рука́ → руки́ (the stress moves). There is no fixed rule. You have to listen and memorise.
